opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to a simple observation: for a long time, generative modeling and representation learning grew up as two separate communities, almost two separate worlds. On the generative side, the default was to train a VAE with a reconstruction objective, compress images into a latent space, and then train a diffusion model in that space. That latent space is very good at preserving pixel detail, but it isn't necessarily semantically meaningful. It doesn't really "understand" what's in the image.

Meanwhile, the representation learning community spent years building very strong visual encoders, through self-supervised learning, contrastive learning, and language supervision. These representations capture structure, objects, and semantics, the things we actually care about when we say a model understands the visual world.

So the question we kept asking was: why does the generative model have to learn all of that from scratch, implicitly, through a denoising objective? In practice, a large part of what a diffusion model is doing during training is learning a decent internal representation. That's expensive and slow, and the representation it ends up with is often weaker than what a dedicated encoder already gives you.

When you align the generative model's internal features with a strong pretrained representation, or go further and treat that representation space itself as the latent space you generate in, a few things happen. Training converges much faster. Generation quality improves. And conceptually it starts to close the loop between understanding and generation, which I think is the more important point.

There's an old belief that if you can generate something, you understand it. I'm not sure that's entirely true. Generation can succeed by modeling low-level statistics very well without much grasp of the underlying structure. I'd rather turn it around: understanding should be the foundation, and generation should be built on top of it. A good representation is like a good map of the world, and generation is just one way of navigating that map.

Longer term, if we want unified models that can perceive, reason, and also imagine or simulate, it doesn't make sense to keep two disconnected latent spaces, one for understanding and one for generation. Using strong representations more directly in generative models is a step toward that kind of unification.

r001.rationale: The response discusses aligning internal features with a pretrained representation, but does not characterize deep supervision as an indirect alignment method.

r002.rationale: It proposes treating the strong representation space itself as the latent space for generation, using it directly as a foundation for the generative model.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short version is: a generative model's job is to learn a mapping from noise to data, and the quality of that mapping depends a lot on how good the intermediate representations are. For a long time we treated generation and representation learning as two separate worlds. On one side you had diffusion models learning to denoise pixels or latents from scratch. On the other side you had self-supervised models like DINO or CLIP that learn really semantic, structured features of images. And the surprising thing is that diffusion models, left to themselves, do eventually learn decent representations, but they learn them slowly and inefficiently, because they're forced to discover semantics as a byproduct of reconstructing low-level details.

So the question we asked was, why make the model rediscover all of that? If you already have a strong visual encoder that knows what a dog looks like, where the object is, how parts relate to each other, you should let the generative model lean on that. In our work on REPA, representation alignment, we just added a simple regularization term that aligns the diffusion transformer's internal features with features from a pretrained encoder. And training became dramatically faster, something like seventeen times fewer steps to reach the same quality, with better final results.

To me the deeper point is that understanding and generation are not really two different problems. If you understand the structure of the visual world, generating it becomes much easier. The bottleneck in generative models often isn't the sampling procedure or the architecture, it's whether the model has a good internal picture of what it's generating. So instead of hoping that emerges from pixel reconstruction, we should inject strong representations directly, and ideally eventually train both sides together so they reinforce each other.

r001.rationale: The response describes a regularization term aligning internal features with a pretrained encoder, but does not characterize deep supervision as an indirect alignment method.

r002.rationale: It proposes injecting strong representations and aligning features, but does not say to use the representation directly as the generative model’s encoder or foundation.

astra-6.text:
I think generation and representation learning are very closely connected, but we often treat them as separate problems. In representation learning, we ask a model to discover the structure of the visual world—what objects are, how parts relate, what stays the same when the appearance changes. A generative model needs to understand those things too, if we want it to produce coherent images.

But when we train a generative model from scratch, we’re asking it to learn all of that implicitly through an objective like denoising. That objective also cares about lots of low-level details. So the model has to learn semantics and synthesize pixels at the same time, without much direct guidance about the underlying structure.

If we already have strong representations, why not use them to guide that learning? Not necessarily to constrain every layer, because generation still needs to preserve details that a recognition model might discard. But to give the model a useful foundation, so it doesn’t have to rediscover everything from scratch.

To me, the interesting question is how to combine that semantic understanding with the flexibility needed for generation. Better representations can help with more than image quality; they may also make the learning process more efficient.

r001.rationale: The response says strong representations could guide learning, but it does not characterize deep supervision as the indirect alignment method.

r002.rationale: It proposes using strong representations to guide generation and give the model a useful foundation, which communicates the foundation approach.

sol-6.1.text:
I think generation and representation learning are closely connected. To generate an image well, a model needs to understand something about its structure—what the objects are, how they relate, and which details matter. But we often ask the generative model to learn all of that from scratch through a denoising objective, even when strong representations are already available.

Why not use those representations more directly? They can provide a useful organizing structure, so the model isn’t spending all its capacity discovering basic semantics while also learning to produce pixels.

The challenge is that a good representation for recognition may discard information that generation needs. It might be invariant to texture or small spatial changes, while a generator has to reconstruct those details. So I don’t think the answer is simply to take any strong encoder and attach a decoder. The interesting question is how to preserve the semantic structure of those representations while retaining enough information for generation.

r001.rationale: The response does not characterize deep supervision or describe an indirect alignment approach.

r002.rationale: It proposes using available strong representations more directly as an organizing structure for the generative model, rather than learning basic semantics from scratch.
